title: Why saving on close loses progress

titles: Why "Save on Close" Loses Your Users' Progress
Don't Save on unload: Use visibilitychange
publish.description: Your app saves progress when the page closes, and on phones it's gone anyway. Why the close event often never fires, and where and when to save instead.
extra: 🎬 The full video (from one laptop to a million students: local storage, progress on the server, 20k writes per second and two devices that disagree) is on the channel.

scenes.heading: Why does *save on close* lose progress?
scenes.narration: Your app saves progress when the user closes the page. Then they close it on a phone, come back, and it's all gone. Why, if the code looks right?

scenes.title: The close event
scenes.narration: The close event is the problem. On phones, the browser often doesn't fire it: the app goes to the background and gets killed, and your code never runs. So save as they go: quiz answers a second after the last change, the video position every few seconds.

steps.note: Backgrounded, then killed: your code never runs
Quiz: 1 s after the last change

scenes.title: The last moment
scenes.narration: And save once more when the page gets hidden: when they switch apps, lock the phone or change tabs. That's the last moment you can count on.

steps.note: The last moment you can count on

scenes.title: One device
scenes.narration: Where does save write? For one device, local storage: a small key value store in the browser that survives closing the tab. On open, it jumps straight back.

scenes.title: Many devices
scenes.narration: To follow the student to their phone, save to your server too. That's a write every few seconds per student. And send the last save as a beacon: a small request the browser keeps sending even as the page goes away.

scenes.title: Save as they go
scenes.narration: Don't trust the close event. Save as they go, and once more when the page gets hidden. How often would you save: every second, or every minute? The full video is on the channel.

notes: Browsers don't guarantee unload or beforeunload, especially on mobile, where apps are backgrounded and later killed without closing. MDN calls visibilitychange (hidden) the last event that's reliably observable by the page.
Unload handlers also make the page ineligible for the back/forward cache in some browsers, so avoiding them makes back navigation faster too.
A debounce alone never fires while a video plays (the position changes all the time), so the position uses an interval and the quiz uses a debounce.
navigator.sendBeacon always sends a POST and can't set custom headers (auth goes in the cookie); fetch with keepalive allows PUT and headers, with a body limit of about 64 KiB.
localStorage is per origin, about 5 MiB, synchronous and strings only; private mode and clearing site data wipe it. Key it by user and clear it on logout on shared computers.
Chrome is deprecating the unload event, another reason not to depend on it. Older Safari (before 14.5) did not fire visibilitychange hidden when closing a tab, so pagehide is a useful fallback.
Safari's tracking prevention can delete script-written storage after 7 days of Safari use without interacting with the site: one more reason to keep a copy on the server.
